Since the problem is NP-hard in general, we focus on analyzing its tractability under the assumption that certain natural parameters of the problem are each bounded by a constant . We consider three parameters: the robustness parameter Γ , the number of distinct due dates in the instance, and the number of jobs with nonzero deviations. Using parameterized-complexity theory, we prove that the problem is W[1]-hard with respect to Γ , but can be solved in XP time with respect to the same parameter. With respect to the number of distinct due dates, we establish a stronger hardness result by showing that the problem remains NP-hard even when there are only two different due dates and is solvable in pseudo-polynomial time when the number of due dates is upper bounded by a constant. To complement these results, we show that the case of a common (single) due date reduces to a robust binary knapsack problem with equal item profits, a problem we prove to be solvable in polynomial time. Finally, we prove that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number of jobs with nonzero deviations.

title: An exact approach for the Train Single-Routing Selection Problem
Repeated near misses and risk perception in newsvendor decisions
Refining demand accuracy for competing retailers
Optimization methods for assigning positions under multiple objectives
abstract: We study a problem arising in the administration of staff positions in organizations with a fixed set of given positions, e.g., public institutions. When a new employee is hired, one or more of the available positions need to be (partially) assigned to her while respecting that they are already (partially) assigned to other staff members, possibly only during certain time intervals. Some positions are better suited for the new hire due to their associated pay grades or other administrative reasons. Furthermore, one seeks an assignment to only few positions and with only few changes over time. This yields a multi-objective optimization problem with a lexicographic objective function that models the mentioned considerations. Our problem can be seen as a scheduling problem with non-availability periods for the machines, where one of the objectives is to minimize the number of job preemptions. We derive structural insights into this problem and present three MIP-formulations based on them. Their solutions are optimal with respect to the three most important sub-objectives and optimal or near-optimal with respect to the least important sub-objective, respectively. We show that, using our formulations, we can find provably optimal solutions considerably faster than with a straightforward approach and near-optimal solutions even faster. In addition, we present a combinatorial algorithm for an important special case of the problem with even better running times. Our results form the backbone of an optimization tool we developed in collaboration with the administration of the Technical University of Munich where it is now used regularly whenever a new employee is hired.

title: Robust optimization for urban metro operations: Solving train timetabling and rolling stock circulation planning problems via facility location models
Tractable conditions for stochastic arbitrage in index options: Theory and evidence
abstract: A stochastic-arbitrage opportunity is present in the equity index options market when a feasible option-enhanced indexed portfolio dominates passive index investment by stochastic dominance under an estimated physical distribution, observed bid–ask prices, and explicit portfolio constraints. We develop and empirically implement the direct use of lower partial co-moment conditions as computationally scalable linear restrictions for constructing such portfolios. While these conditions appear in earlier work as analytical necessary first-order conditions, we show that they provide an exact necessary and sufficient characterization of the stochastic-arbitrage portfolio problem under co-monotonicity of the option-enhanced payoff and the index value, which is induced by an established position limit allowing at most one option position per unit of index exposure. This exact characterization substantially reduces problem size and computation time, allowing fine discretization, large-scale backtesting, and extensive robustness analysis without specialized computing resources. Using this framework, we test for stochastic-arbitrage opportunities in one-month S&P 500 index options. Out-of-sample tests indicate such opportunities in high-volatility regimes, predominantly in the form of call front spreads, when portfolio construction accounts for time variation in the market risk premium and negative conditional skewness of index returns. The qualitative findings are robust across alternative density forecasts, data treatments, and optimization specifications, while no comparable evidence is found in low- or medium-volatility regimes.

title: Pattern-based adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm for roll-on roll-off vehicle routing problem
Strategic adoption of 3D printing in multi-product supply chains: cost and capacity considerations
abstract: This paper explores the integration of Additive Manufacturing (or 3D printing) into decentralized supply chains, focusing on the strategic decisions manufacturers and retailers make when facing capacity constraints. Using a Stackelberg game framework, we analyze how AM impacts traditional wholesale pricing across two scenarios. First, a manufacturer producing two distinct products and second, a case involving multiple products, each affected by AM's capacity limitations. For the first scenario, we derive sufficient conditions to find the equilibrium under a generic demand distribution, and for a uniform distribution, we fully derive the equilibrium and identify the critical cost threshold below which AM adoption is preferable. For the second scenario, we determine the conditions for the equilibrium, offering insights into the feasibility of AM relative to traditional manufacturing. Furthermore, we find that, contrary to some literature, even when AM incurs higher per-unit costs than traditional methods, it remains viable for some supply chains. However, limited AM capacity, particularly under high demand, may restrict its adoption, highlighting capacity constraints as a pivotal factor in AM decision-making. This study extends current research by examining multi-product and capacity-driven scenarios, providing valuable guidance for supply chain managers weighing the benefits of traditional manufacturing against those of AM.

title: Integrated berth allocation and yard assignment with conflict-induced preemptive operations in bulk cargo ports
Robust e-waste recycling facility location problem with decision-dependent uncertain customer behavior
Parameterized complexity of scheduling problems in robotic process automation
abstract: This paper studies the growing domain of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) problems. Motivated by scheduling problems arising in RPA, we study the parameterized complexity of the single-machine problem with precedence constraints, release times, and deadlines (i.e., the problem known as 1 ⁢ | p r e c , 𝑟 𝑗 , 𝑑 𝑗 | ∗ in the three-field notation). We focus on parameters naturally linked to RPA systems, including chain-like precedences, the number of distinct processing times, and the structure of the time windows. We show that the problem is strongly XNLP -hard parameterized by the number of chains, even with only two prescribed processing times and two distinct time-window lengths. The problem remains XNLP -hard even under prec-consistent time windows. On the positive side, we obtain polynomial-time algorithm when all jobs share a single time-window length and FPT when the processing times, release times and deadlines are chain-uniform. We also show that the problem lies in XNLP when parameterized by the width of the precedence relation either when the instance is encoded in unary or the processing times are bounded.

title: Pros and cons of service pooling considering price and congestion-sensitive service users
Semi-strong efficiency schemes and indexes for arbitrary technologies with compact dominating sets
abstract: An efficiency scheme is a general optimization program that encompasses a large category of various specific efficiency indexes or measures. This theoretical paper establishes general results for three weak schemes: the input/output-variables scheme, the slack-variables scheme and the Russell-type scheme. The optimization programs offer a unified analysis of the entire category of efficiency indexes that are characterized by semi-strictly monotone improvement functions as objectives. It includes all common strong measures, but also many weak ones, especially the oriented (non-graph) slacks-based measures and the radial models of data envelopment analysis (DEA). The paper demonstrates that the three schemes produce equivalent, well-defined efficiency indexes when the improvement functions are specified accordingly. Several useful general theorems are proven for technologies with compact dominating sets of the assessed production activities. In general, the technologies do not need to satisfy any further properties on disposability, convexity, scalability, closeness or boundedness and may even be discrete. The findings are illustrated by numerical examples and are concretized by specific technologies and improvement functions that lead to the standard DEA models and to unoriented biradial efficiency indexes. In particular, the radial DEA models, known as path-based measures, are slacks-based as well.

title: Collaborative routing problems in automated warehouses
abstract: The pick-and-drive system is a novel solution for warehouse automation. It integrates two types of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Storage and supply AMRs (S-AMRs) navigate to a storage area, where they lift unit loads and transport them to a disposition area. Picking AMRs (P-AMRs) move freely within this disposition area. They carry bins and meet S-AMRs to collect items from the unit loads attached to the S-AMRs by means of robotic arms. We take an operational perspective on the pick-and-drive system and focus on the problem of determining and scheduling meeting locations and sequences of the AMRs, so that all required items are picked. This setting is interpreted as a vehicle routing problem, where the customers (S-AMRs) collaborate with the vehicles (P-AMRs). We consider two objective functions, minimizing the total distance driven by the AMRs and minimizing the sum of completion times of the P-AMRs. We translate these routing problems into a mathematical framework and provide theoretical insights by examining a specific case where the potential meeting points lie along a line. For this scenario, we present an approximation algorithm for the case of minimizing the overall distance traveled and demonstrate that minimizing the sum of completion times is strongly NP-complete. Additionally, we prove strong NP-completeness of the general case when minimizing the overall distance traveled. Leveraging the structural insights, we develop heuristics that are evaluated in a numerical study. Our results highlight the potential impact of the system in practice.

title: When blockchain creates value? Financial leasing for the newsvendor under data source uncertainty
Scheduling of cooperative twin yard cranes under bidirectional container flows
Fifty years of Robust Linear and Convex Optimization
abstract: During the last 25 years Robust Linear and Convex Optimization (RLCO) has become an important subfield in optimization after several seminal publications in the late nineties. Several papers published during 1973–1997 already contain some of the ingredients of modern RLCO. In this paper, we describe the contributions of these papers during the first 25 years, and we describe the main achievements of modern RLCO during the last 25 years. We focus on generic principles and methodology.

title: Optimal allocation of embedding dimensions under finite-sample constraints
abstract: The embedding dimension of categorical predictors is usually selected through heuristic tuning, although it directly affects model complexity, approximation quality, and finite-sample generalization. This paper formulates embedding dimension selection as a constrained allocation problem. The main contribution is to show that embedding capacity can be allocated across heterogeneous categorical predictors according to an explicit approximation–estimation tradeoff. We characterize approximation error through the singular-value tail of the latent category representation, while estimation error increases with total embedding complexity. Under a fixed global embedding budget and a tractable approximation model, this leads to a closed-form allocation rule in which the dimension assigned to each predictor is proportional to the square root of its approximation value relative to its parameter cost. Simulation experiments support the proposed approximation–estimation interpretation and show that the allocation rule improves budget efficiency relative to standard uniform and cardinality-based heuristics, particularly when the budget is binding and predictor heterogeneity is substantial. A real-data healthcare application further shows improvements in predictive accuracy and probabilistic calibration. Overall, the results establish embedding-dimension allocation as a principled finite-sample optimization problem rather than a purely heuristic modeling choice.

title: Sorting under multiple eyes: A multi-view preference learning framework for multi-criteria decision aiding
A new critical realist approach for evaluating multimethodological practice in operational research
abstract: Understanding why practitioners take the actions they do in multimethodological operational research (OR), and the effects these actions have, is fundamental for evaluating and improving practice. But it is widely recognized in OR literature and amongst practitioners that objective, comparative evaluation of complex, real-world interventions is challenging if not impossible. It is not clear how multimethodology should be evaluated. Critical realism has been advocated for exploring causation to evaluate OR practice holistically, but not fully operationalized. For our collaborative research evaluating multimethodological practice supporting strategic decision-making in non-academic settings, we therefore developed a new approach. We synthesized and operationalized empirical research and theories in OR and recent developments in critical realism and social science. In this paper, we present our theoretical framework – a new critical realist ontology of multimethodological OR practice and methodologies – and our empirical research design. We illustrate the approach with a case study of an OR analysis for a business case for government investment in a national capability. We demonstrate how we investigated the intervention context and the complex process of practitioners’ choice of methods using interviews and project documents, thematic and comparative analysis, rich description, and structural and causal analysis. We explore how this new operationalization of critical realism for identifying and comparing causal mechanisms across practitioner case studies can be used: (1) to examine mechanisms leading to other actions and outcomes, including intervention success; and (2) to theorize and evaluate mixed methods research projects across disciplines, including their causal complexity and practical utility.

title: Optimization-based strategic planning for geographical healthcare accessibility in developing countries: A literature review
abstract: Access to healthcare facilities is a critical issue in developing countries, where limited resources and significant challenges hinder progress toward universal health coverage, one of the targets pursued by the United Nations. As a result, the Operations Research (OR) community has become increasingly active in addressing this issue, employing various techniques, particularly optimization. However, making long-term strategic decisions remains challenging, as these often require substantial investments and directly affect large populations. Moreover, much of the existing literature is predominantly theoretical. This paper reviews studies published over the past two decades that use optimization techniques to inform strategic planning decisions aimed at improving healthcare accessibility and specifically contain a case study conducted in a developing country. The review explores the nature of the problems tackled, considering factors such as the level of care, service delivery channels, objectives, criteria, or potential hierarchy and multi-period settings. Additionally, we discuss the modeling approaches, solution methodologies, and the extent of practical implementation. The goal of this survey is not only to summarize existing work but also to provide a roadmap for future research, offering valuable insights for OR practitioners in the field.

title: Route and schedule adjustment for liner shipping service under anticipated disruption events
Long memory score-driven models as approximations for rough Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes
Counting operations to analyze and compare Fast DEA procedures
A dynamic programming algorithm for the Robotic Cell Problem with a fixed job processing order
abstract: The Robotic Cell Problem (RCP) is a flow-shop scheduling problem in which jobs must be transferred from each machine to the next one by a robot. The robot movements require non-negligible time and must be optimized to minimize the makespan. The problem is practically relevant in the context of manufacturing systems. In this work, we study a variant of the RCP in which the processing order of the jobs is fixed. We present a dynamic programming algorithm for the exact optimization of this variant and show how it can be transformed into an accurate heuristic. Computational results are provided on instances with up to 30 jobs and 15 machines under different distributions of travel and processing times. The results indicate that our algorithm can solve significantly larger instances than existing methods. The proposed approach may also serve as a subroutine within future heuristic methods for the general RCP.

title: The double-edged role of manufacturer corporate social responsibility: How selling formats and store brand entry shape platform-based supply chains
Robust and fair ticket allocation under strategic passenger behavior for enhancing railway system resilience
Outsourcing under cost information asymmetry and tariffs pressure: When multinationals prefer their local competitors
To cooperate with Top-tier streamers or not? A sequential bargaining approach in live-streaming supply chains
A unified learning framework for the block relocation problem: A new performance baseline
The impact of resale price maintenance on a legitimate retailer’s decision to sell counterfeits in dual-channel competition
Two-stage one-dimensional cutting stock problem with flexible item sizes in steel industry
Exact methods for disabling interdiction problems
abstract: Interdiction problems are a class of adversarial combinatorial optimisation problems where two agents compete to optimise the same objective function in opposite directions. In this work, we focus on the case in which the leader disables a subset of elements from the instance, preventing their use in the follower’s solution. We introduce methodological improvements for three existing methods, providing a tighter version of two Benders decompositions and a generalised version of a covering decomposition which exploit the availability of super-optimal bounds. Such bounds are obtained through three novel heuristic methods based on a bi-objective auxiliary problem that generates diverse, high-quality solutions for the follower, in order to reduce computation times. The framework is applied to the Shortest Path Interdiction Problem and the Set Covering Interdiction Problem. The experimental results suggest that the proposed approaches outperform the existing Benders decompositions and perform comparably with the basic covering decomposition, but scale better for large sizes and interdiction budgets.

title: Learning-driven multi-start local search for the multiple row equal facility layout problem
abstract: Given a set of facilities, integer numbers k and r , a facility flow matrix, and a group distance matrix, the multiple row equal facility layout problem (MREFLP) aims to determine a facility-to-group assignment with the minimum aggregate of the products of the flow cost and the facility distances, such that the number of the facilities assigned to each group does not exceed r . The MREFLP is a general model for various applications including operating theater layout in hospitals. However, due to its NP-hardness, solving this problem is computationally difficult. This paper proposes an effective learning-driven multi-start local search algorithm for this problem, which features a learning-driven solution construction procedure and a dedicated two-phase local search. Experiments on 572 benchmark instances demonstrate that the algorithm surpasses the state-of-the-art algorithms. Specifically, it achieves 165 new upper bounds and 407 equal results (including 289 known optima). An ablation study is performed to show the influence of each algorithm component.

title: Condition-based maintenance for multi-component systems under spatio-temporal degradation propagation
Covariance matrix estimation for positively correlated assets
abstract: The comovement phenomenon in financial markets creates decision scenarios with positively correlated asset returns. This paper addresses covariance matrix estimation under such conditions, motivated by observations of significant positive correlations in factor-sorted portfolio monthly returns. We demonstrate that fine-tuning eigenvectors linked to weak factors within rotation-equivariant frameworks produces well-conditioned covariance matrix estimates. Our Eigenvector Rotation Shrinkage Estimator (ERSE) pairwise rotates eigenvectors while preserving orthogonality, equivalent to performing multiple linear shrinkage on two distinct eigenvalues. Empirical results on factor-sorted portfolios from the Ken French data library demonstrate that ERSE outperforms existing rotation-equivariant estimators in reducing out-of-sample portfolio variance, achieving average risk reductions of 10.52\% versus linear shrinkage methods and 12.46\% versus nonlinear shrinkage methods. Further checks indicate that ERSE yields covariance matrices with lower condition numbers, produces more concentrated and stable portfolio weights, and provides consistent improvements across different subperiods and estimation windows.

title: Decision-focused learning for distributionally robust multi-agent dynamic vehicle routing in e-commerce last-mile delivery
Surge pricing and multi-agency interaction in humanitarian logistics: An equilibrium approach
Platform contracts for emission-reducing smart products with consumers’ privacy concern
When manufacturer encroachment backfires: Effects of cross-selling in Internet of Things product supply chains
Fast but reliable? Consistency of preference elicitation with ranking and rating for multicriteria decision analysis in Real‑World cases
abstract: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) methods require stakeholder preference elicitation, but standard approaches like Swing weight elicitation can be time-consuming and cognitively demanding for practical applications. This study investigated whether fast preference elicitation methods—direct ranking and rating of objectives—can effectively substitute for rigorous Swing weight elicitation in real-world public decision-making contexts. Data were collected from three case studies involving flood early warning system development in West Africa and wastewater management transitions in two Swiss rural communities. Individual stakeholder preferences for objectives were elicited through ranking, rating, and Swing weight methods across multiple workshops. Consistency between ranking and rating was high for most stakeholders (median γ-values around -0.9). Weights derived from objectives ranking correlated better with Swing weights than rating weights, particularly in the largest case study. When aggregated across stakeholders, fast elicitation methods implemented in MCDA produced nearly identical rankings of alternatives compared to Swing weights (Kendall's τ > 0.84), with no rank reversals in top-5 alternatives between weights derived from objectives ranking and Swing. However, holistic, direct ranking of alternatives showed poor correlation with MCDA-calculated rankings (τ < 0.5), supporting value-focused thinking principles. These findings demonstrate that fast ranking of objectives can approximate Swing weight elicitation outcomes while significantly reducing time and cognitive burden, offering a practical approach for consensus-seeking in resource-constrained public decision processes.

title: Agency vs. resale: Selling format choice on competing platforms with asymmetric suppliers
Deep reinforcement learning for aging cheese inventory management under correlated prices
abstract: In aging cheese inventory management, producers must account for auto-regressive and correlated prices, both for raw milk at the purchasing side and for age-differentiated final products at the sales market side. Purchasing decisions determine the youngest additions to the multi-age inventory system. In production decisions, amelioration effects entail a trade-off between immediate revenues and further maturation. Producers have operational flexibility in issuance decisions because the age printed on the packaging represents only the minimum maturation time, allowing for deliberate excess. We solve the aging cheese inventory problem using deep reinforcement learning (DRL), as the problem size grows exponentially with the number of inventory age classes. However, state-of-the-art actor-critic DRL algorithms face difficulties when dealing with the high-dimensional action spaces induced by issuance flexibility. We introduce and analyze three possible remedies. First, we consider action space dimensionality reduction by curtailing issuance flexibility. The second approach also reduces dimensionality via actor pipelining, allowing issuance actions to be replaced with heuristic rules. Third, we analyze multi-agent actor architectures that distribute learning across multiple neural networks. Our results show that dimensionality reduction via pipelining achieves the best trade-off between policy quality and computational effort. Overall, action dimensionality reduction is both more effective and more efficient than multi-agent designs. Compared to a myopic rolling-horizon planning benchmark, our DRL policies increase profits by 16.7%, on average. Moreover, modeling the cheese-specific price dynamics is essential. Policies trained under simplified price assumptions yield profit losses of 6.7%, on average. In full factorial experiments, we investigate the effect of key price process parameters: mean reversion speed, volatility, and correlation of purchase and sales prices. In contrast to prior work, we find that issuance flexibility provides notable profit gains only in highly volatile, fast mean-reverting price environments.

title: Competitive implications of spectrum subleasing on pricing, quality and sourcing decisions
From global to local? Designing optimal climate-linked industrial policy for global supply chains under sustainability gaps
abstract: In developed countries, local sourcing is typically more expensive than global alternatives due to sustainability gaps in supplier carbon intensity. Climate policies seek to promote cleaner inputs through incentives such as consumer tax credits, but their effectiveness on economic efficiency and climate externalities remains uncertain. To address this, we develop a game-theoretical model of a local original equipment manufacturer (OEM) that allocates orders between a less sustainable, cost-efficient global supplier and a more sustainable, costlier local supplier, subject to a government-imposed eligibility threshold that conditions consumer tax credits. Our analysis reveals a non-decreasing, three-zone structure for the optimal threshold: it starts at zero in emerging markets, rises gradually in transitional markets, and maximizes in mature markets. Complete localization arises only when the sustainability gap is narrow, while wider gaps restrict thresholds to an interior value to avoid disengagement. Stricter thresholds always increase economic surplus, but emission reductions occur only in intermediate-scale markets, especially when supplier sustainability differs substantially. Extending the model to competitive settings, we find that under global competition, localization policies take effect sooner but reach the maximum value more slowly, while local competition accelerates both the initiation and finalization of the localization process. Competition also alters economic and environmental effects: economic efficiency initially declines with market growth before recovering, and stricter thresholds fail to reduce emissions due to either policy exemptions or reduced output responsiveness. These results underscore that effective climate policy must be adaptive and aligned with market maturity, competition, and supplier characteristics.

title: Permutation tests on common production frontiers in nonparametric models
abstract: Permutation techniques, which involve recomputing a test statistic over permutations of data, have a long history in statistics and have become increasingly useful with the availability of greater computational power. However, until now, there have been no permutation tests available for statistical analysis within non-parametric models for production frontiers. We develop new permutation-based tests for comparing production technologies. These tests can be used to determine general differences between production technologies and to assess whether one production possibility set is nested within another. They can be applied both for comparison of frontiers for independent groups and for analysing frontier shifts across time for panel data. Our permutation tests all make use of Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) for estimating efficiencies, and indirectly the production possibility set, through linear programming. The tests are easily implementable. We show that our suggested permutations of the observations satisfy the necessary randomisation assumptions, and hereby that the tests have the desired sizes and, consequently, are exact. Further we show that our tests are consistent. The main advantage of permutation tests is that they are particularly useful for relatively small samples. However, one needs to be careful about the hypotheses that are being tested.

title: A new cut-and-solve-based approach for the single-source capacitated facility location problem
abstract: The Single-Source Capacitated Facility Location Problem involves locating facilities so that each customer’s demand is met by a single facility and capacity constraints are not violated. This paper focuses on developing an exact algorithm to handle this problem. In this sense, we propose an algorithm that uses four strategies: (i) strengthening the problem formulation through a cutting-plane procedure; (ii) exploiting partial linear relaxations to obtain good lower bounds; (iii) applying a heuristic to obtain a good upper bound; and (iv) applying a Cut-and-Solve-based scheme to construct a binary search tree. We evaluate and select cutting-plane generation procedures that differ from those previously used for the problem and propose a new heuristic procedure. The results of the computational experiments showed that the proposed algorithm found a greater or equal number of optimal values with lower runtime than the state-of-the-art exact algorithm in 22 out of 26 subsets, and than the CPLEX solver in 19 out of 26 subsets.

title: Strategic cooperation: Winning in live-streaming e-commerce with key opinion leaders
abstract: In live-streaming e-commerce, brands, Key Opinion Leaders (KOLs), and social platforms must make complex decisions about collaboration structures, balancing sales incentives against the risk of long-term reputation loss. Using differential game theory, this paper investigates three cooperation modes in a three-echelon social e-commerce supply chain: the independent-KOL mode, the brand-signing KOL mode, and the platform-signing KOL mode. Our findings indicate that when the live-streaming promotion effect is relatively strong, a higher KOL commission rate enhances brand goodwill when the reputation loss effect is relatively weak, but diminishes brand goodwill when the reputation loss effect is relatively strong. Moreover, the brand-signing mode enhances brand goodwill and KOL influence when both platform and KOL commission rates are relatively low. Conversely, when these rates exceed certain thresholds, the platform-signing mode becomes more advantageous and expands market demand. Additionally, signing a KOL accelerates profit growth for the signing parties, while non-signing members can also benefit from others' cooperative arrangements. Finally, the brand- or platform-signing KOL modes yield higher total cooperative profit than the independent-KOL mode when live-streaming efficiency is lower, whereas the opposite holds when efficiency is higher. These results offer strategic guidance for brand managers and platform operators in optimizing partnership structures and mitigating the dynamic risks inherent in KOL live-streaming.

title: Applying Distributionally Robust Optimization frameworks to tackle travel-time uncertainty in the ambulance location and dispatching problem
abstract: The efficient management of Emergency Medical Services (EMS) relies on the strategic location of ambulances and their optimal dispatching, two decisions that are inherently challenged by considerable uncertainty. This paper addresses the ambulance location and dispatching problem under uncertain travel times, a factor often overlooked in the literature that nonetheless plays a critical role in response times. Travel-time uncertainty is represented by a finite, data-driven set of candidate probability distributions fitted to historical data. On this set we build three distribution-aware frameworks: a min–max model over the candidate set (Distributionally Robust Optimization), a model that averages performance over the set (Distributionally Stochastic Optimization), and a scenario-robust extension (Distributionally scenario Robust Optimization). The performance of the solutions they produced to a manageable subset of scenarios (in-sample experiments) is evaluated on different realizations of travel-time uncertainty (out-of-sample experiments) constructed on historical data from the EMS in the Basque Country (Spain). The results highlight the importance of explicitly modeling travel-time uncertainty in EMS system design. Finally, a Discrete Event Simulation model allows assessing the behavior of those solutions when the spatial and temporal variability of emergency call patterns are incorporated. The distribution-aware solutions align with Stochastic Optimization in similar average response time while improving the response time attained under the most adverse candidate distribution, and they avoid the conservatism of Robust Optimization.

title: Minimum risk consensus model based on consensus breakdown probability
Privacy-preserving multi-source transfer learning for credit risk prediction with mixture cure models
Integrated deployment and operational planning of offshore wind–aquaculture coupled systems
Beyond the pitch: An integrated machine learning and operations research methodology for financially sustainable squad formation
Inter-terminal collaboration: Optimizing multi-terminal berth allocation with container ground transfers
Original equipment manufacturer’s sourcing strategy with production cost information asymmetry
abstract: Sourcing is a strategic decision for original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). We study an OEM choosing between insourcing and outsourcing to a contract manufacturer (CM) that privately knows its production cost and sells a competing product. Because sourcing precedes wholesale pricing, the OEM must anticipate the CM’s wholesale price signal about its cost type. Costless separation reproduces the perfect-information outcome, whereas costly separation and pooling raise the OEM’s expected acquisition cost, reduce outsourcing profit, and contract cost-saving outsourcing. Their effects on strategic outsourcing depend on changes in the sourcing threshold and feasible upper boundary separating strategic from cost-saving outsourcing. Costly separation widens strategic outsourcing when the feasibility boundary does not bind, narrows it when the boundary binds under both information structures, and may have either effect when it binds only under asymmetric information. Under pooling, the strategic outsourcing width and share depend on the movements of two boundaries. A benchmark with a noncompeting CM shows why downstream competition matters: without it, private cost information leaves both sourcing boundaries unchanged. The CM benefits from cost opacity only in a high-price pooling region and when its own-brand product is sufficiently competitive, because wholesale and retail margin gains can exceed demand loss. Whenever cost opacity distorts the signaling outcome, it reduces the OEM’s profit, consumer surplus, and total supply chain profit. A transfer payment can induce disclosure when the CM prefers opacity. These results show how cost signaling changes whether the OEM outsources and whether outsourcing is motivated by cost savings or downstream competition.

title: Evaluating dynamic efficiency: Multi-layer dynamic non-radial data envelopment analysis with time-lagged effect structure
abstract: Economic systems are inherently dynamic, often characterised by temporal lags between the firms’ resource inputs and the realisation of outcomes. Static data envelopment analysis (DEA) approaches, which are widely used in efficiency measurement, largely overlook these intertemporal dynamics. While existing dynamic DEA frameworks account for temporal dependence, they typically capture limited source of efficiency variation and are unable to simultaneously accommodate time-lagged effect, data heterogeneity and the asymmetric contributions of individual inputs. As a result, such models may yield misleading efficiency benchmarks. To address these limitations, this study set up a multi-layer dynamic non-radial DEA (ML-DNRDEA) model that accommodates time-lagged interdependencies and non-proportional input adjustments in efficiency measurement. We adopt the ML-DNRDEA to assess efficiency in the technology industry using a completed panel of 1190 firm-year observations from 2012 to 2021. The results demonstrate that production delay effects have a significant impact on technical efficiency (TE) assessment, with the underlying drivers of TE variation differing across sub-industries. In particular, in the Semiconductors and Software sub-industries, production delays primarily operate through scale efficiency (SE), whereas in IT Services and Technology Hardware , pure technical efficiency (PTE) is more strongly affected. Moreover, the contribution of individual inputs to efficiency is asymmetric rather than proportional. The proposed ML-DNRDEA model provides more granular sources of inefficiency, such as intertemporal dependence and input-specific effects, providing managers and policymakers with richer diagnostic information to support informed decision-making and policy design.

title: A metaheuristic algorithm for locomotive rescheduling in freight transportation under disruptions
abstract: We address a weekly Locomotive Rescheduling Problem (LResP) in the context of rail freight transportation, based on the real-life Austrian setting, in the event of severe disruptions. The main objective is to minimize trip cancellations and deviations from the original plan while meeting locomotive availability and maintenance constraints. To solve LResP, we design a Multi-Neighborhood Search metaheuristic (MNS) that effectively combines both traditional and problem-tailored neighborhoods. The proposed MNS relies on stochastic exploration and uses a simulated annealing scheme to guide the search. In addition, for a comparative analysis, we define a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation that significantly extends a model from the literature for the planning problem by incorporating a new objective function and additional constraints required for the rescheduling setting. We tested the proposed approaches on instances from a real-world setting of the Austrian railways under severe disruptions. While a few good-quality feasible solutions can be obtained for small-scale instances by solving the MILP model with a general-purpose solver, MNS is both fast and scalable, obtaining good quality solutions on instances with thousands of trips, thus highlighting its reliability and applicability in real-world scenarios.

title: Static resource allocation: Maximizing revenue and ensuring fairness
abstract: In this study, we focus on a static multi-resource allocation problem where customers pay to obtain resources from which they derive utility. Resources can be allocated either dynamically, over time, or statically, in a single-shot process. In this study, we explore the trade-off between revenue and fairness in a static setting. We distinguish between fairness-aware decision makers, who prioritize fairness among allocations with equal revenue, and fairness-unaware ones, who randomly select an allocation among all revenue-maximizing options. When the number of customers exceeds the number of available resources, we prove that fairness can be achieved without any revenue loss, but only under fairness-aware decision-making. In contrast, fairness-unaware decision makers are at high risk of selecting allocations with substantially lower fairness, despite achieving the same revenue. We also find that both fairness and revenue are maximized when customers have low price sensitivity and prefer more expensive resources. In contrast, when resources outnumber customers, trade-offs between fairness and revenue become inevitable, especially when customers are highly price-sensitive and prefer cheaper options. In our numerical experiments, we also study the impact of merging resource categories and heterogeneity in customer preferences on the revenue-fairness trade-off. Finally, we complement these analyses with an empirically calibrated case study, showing that our fairness insights remain robust in realistic allocation settings.

title: Robust Dynamic Network Data Envelopment Analysis for Supply Chain Performance Evaluation
abstract: Supply chains pose a challenging performance assessment problem because decentralised decision-making creates trade-offs between system- and firm-level objectives, exacerbated by intertemporal effects from inventory accumulation and demand fluctuations, task heterogeneity such as product differentiation, and competitive–cooperative interactions that impose system-level constraints. To address this challenge, this paper develops a dynamic network data envelopment analysis (DN-DEA) framework with robust counterparts, based on three complementary perspectives on supply chains: strategic behavioural, intertemporal and competitive-cooperative. We extend DN-DEA to cost-minimising networks, enabling a Farrell-style decomposition of cost efficiency into technical and allocative components, while linking system-, firm- and plant-level performance in a networked and dynamic setting. Robust formulations account for typical data perturbations in supply chains, protecting efficiency estimates from uncertainty. Applied to detailed panel data from a pulp and packaging supply chain, the approach decomposes efficiency into system- and firm-level components, demonstrates how dynamics affect efficiency rankings over time, and shows that robustness substantially reduces rank volatility, providing actionable insights for supply chain performance measurement and coordination.

title: Channel operations and performance improvement of a green supply chain considering risk aversion and carbon abatement
Competitive distribution channel strategies in three-tier supply chains with horizontal product differentiation
Leveraging 0–1 linear programming for partitioning and sampling in simulation-based optimization: The case of nested partitions
abstract: Discrete Simulation-based Optimization (DSO) problems typically involve highly complex stochastic systems such as urban road networks or electric grid networks. For such problems, computing the value of the objective function requires computationally intensive simulations. Many solution methods rely on iteratively sampling and partitioning the feasible space to progressively concentrate the sampling effort on its most promising portions. To boost the effectiveness of such methods, it is fundamental to quickly identify which portions of the feasible space are relevant to explore through an effective partitioning scheme. In this paper, we focus on binary DSO problems and introduce Nested Clusters, an enhancement of Nested Partitions that leverages the mathematical formulation of the feasible space to construct auxiliary 0–1 linear programming formulations for partitioning and sampling. Additionally, we expand Nested Clusters by introducing a biasing technique that improves the average quality of the sampled solutions, boosting the overall performance. Finally, we apply Nested Clusters to a simulation-based charger location problem for an autonomous fleet of ride-hailing taxis in New York City, which serves as our primary benchmark. We conduct further controlled synthetic tests on four binary simulation–optimization problems spanning different combinatorial structures and stochastic evaluators. On the tested ride-hailing charger-location instances, both proposed partitioning and biased sampling strategies independently improve solution quality relative to Nested Partitions; combining them yields an average 2.2% improvement in the best solutions found.

title: Optimization under uncertainty for energy infrastructure planning: A synthesis of methods, tools, and open challenges
abstract: Energy infrastructure planning under uncertainty has become increasingly complex as electrification, interdependence between energy carriers, decarbonization, and extreme weather events reshape long-term investment decisions. This paper surveys recent advances at the intersection of generation and transmission expansion, and optimization under uncertainty, with a focus on stochastic programming, robust optimization, and distributionally robust optimization. We then categorize modeling needs along the axes of modeling fidelity, uncertainty characterization, and solution methods to identify dominant modeling features and trace research gaps. We further examine emerging directions at the interface of optimization and machine learning, including forecasting, scenario generation, and learned surrogates and discuss how these tools can be embedded within infrastructure planning models.

title: Trust builder or defensive moat? Blockchain adoption and incentive mechanisms in a food supply chain with asymmetric competition
Trustworthy AI and risk-aware planning for global supply chains: A probabilistic framework with knowledge graph constraints
abstract: Global artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled supply chains (SCs) face AI-induced risks, such as bias in AI-driven decisions and the resulting erosion of trust. Despite extensive research on mitigation of AI-related risks using digital twins, Bayesian risk models, and graph optimization in isolation, the literature lacks a unified framework for jointly modelling and mitigating interconnected AI-induced risks. To this end, we propose an integrated framework underpinned by a knowledge-graph (KG)-constrained generative probabilistic planning approach that incorporates a risk-aware reward function and supply-chain trust propagation while leveraging a digital twin for cascading-failure stress testing. Using DataCo data comprising 180,519 transactions across 43 countries, we compare the proposed framework against six benchmarks: static, Bayesian, digital-twin, pure reinforcement learning (RL), component-isolation RL, and robust risk-averse. The results show that the proposed approach delivers the lowest overall weighted objective and lowest critical-failure rate across all evaluated policies. The findings offer three managerial insights: (i) adaptive, probabilistic risk-mitigation approaches outperform fixed rules as AI-driven risk and trust conditions shift in global supply chains; (ii) incorporating trust into decision rules helps managers decide when AI actions can proceed automatically and when human review is required; and (iii) monitoring disparity indicators, such as differences in delivery-risk exposure across regions or customer groups, allows fairness considerations to be assessed alongside operational performance.

title: Increased scheduling flexibility for multi-league sports scheduling
A two-stage optimization framework for maintenance depot location and technician allocation in urban rail transit systems
Single machine optimistic bilevel scheduling problems with selection: State-of-the-art and new results
abstract: We consider bilevel optimization for machine scheduling problems where two agents, the leader and the follower, take decisions on the same jobset. We survey the somewhat limited relevant literature, and thereafter we present a large set of new complexity results, focusing on single machine bilevel scheduling in the context of optimistic setting. Here, the leader acts first with the aim of selecting a subset of jobs to optimize his/her own objective function. Next, the follower schedules these selected jobs in order to optimize a given criterion. The optimistic setting is such that, among all his/her optimal solutions, the follower returns the one that is minimum for the leader’s objective function. We consider several basic scheduling criteria for both the leader and the follower and establish the complexity of the corresponding problems.

title: Integrating response time and attention duration in Bayesian preference learning for multiple criteria decision aiding
Structural concentration in weighted networks: A class of topology-aware indices
Multi-visit truck-drone pickup and delivery problem with release dates and drone resupply
Minimizing network development costs using reverse p-median models
abstract: The reverse p-median problem seeks network modifications that improve the accessibility of predetermined facility locations subject to budget and network-design constraints. Solving this problem on general networks with discrete edge length choices is computationally challenging because shortest-path distances must be repeatedly recalculated across a large number of feasible network configurations. To address this challenge, we develop a globally optimal solution framework, called the Reverse p-Median Solver (RPM), which combines structured enumeration with two complementary search procedures to efficiently explore the feasible budget domain. A key feature of RPM is its ability to identify globally optimal networks over the entire feasible budget range and construct the corresponding Pareto-efficient frontier between network cost and investment budget, enabling decision-makers to systematically evaluate trade-offs between infrastructure investment and network performance. Computational experiments on illustrative electricity-grid examples and a large-scale transportation network case study in Virginia demonstrate the practical applicability and scalability of the proposed framework.

title: A new perspective on multi-objective project scheduling problems: Evaluating with multiple reference profiles
abstract: This paper addresses the multi-objective resource-constrained project scheduling problem (MORCPSP) under a non-compensatory preference structure over conflicting objectives. From the decision maker’s perspective, objectives reflecting distinct stakeholder concerns (such as minimising project tardiness and minimising resource leveling cost) often exhibit a non-compensatory relationship, in which good performance on one objective cannot fully offset unacceptable performance on the other. This characteristic makes it difficult for decision makers to specify precise compensatory weights between objectives. Moreover, existing multi-objective heuristic algorithms (MOHAs) typically generate large sets of non-dominated schedules without using preference information during the search, thereby leaving decision makers with the burden of selecting from numerous alternative schedules. To address these limitations, we develop MOHA-EMP, a preference-guided framework that integrates the Evaluating with Multiple Reference Profiles (EMP) procedure into the fitness evaluation and selection of the evolutionary search. Computational experiments conducted on 2700 RanGen2 instances and 480 PSPLIB J30 instances show MOHA-EMP achieves higher preference satisfaction than its standard MOHA counterparts for five benchmarking MOHAs (NSGA-II, ECGA, NTGA2, bNTGA and MOEA/D), improving the average EMP-measure by 12.5%–27.1% while reducing the number of output schedules by 89%–95%. The sensitivity analysis further shows that the method remains robust under varying project sizes, deadlines, resource constraints and network structures. These findings indicate the broad applicability of preference-integrated evolutionary search for decision support in MORCPSP.

A DeepSets-guided scheduling framework for total tardiness minimization in single-machine scheduling
abstract: We present the DeepSets-Guided Scheduling Framework (DGSF), a hybrid machine learning and optimization framework for the single-machine total tardiness scheduling problem with release times. DGSF employs a geometric instance-classification rule to characterize scheduling instances using aggregate structural parameters. This classification enables targeted machine learning models to be trained across diverse instance types while leveraging training on smaller instances within the same instance class. The machine learning model is designed to accommodate varying numbers of jobs and uses attention to combine each job’s features with information about the other jobs, learning priorities that reflect their relationships. These priorities define an initial sequence, which is refined through local swaps and restricted optimization to generate high-quality schedules. Computational tests show that DGSF generates better solutions than the tested heuristics for instances with all jobs released at time zero; and near optimal solutions (within 0.65–2.56%) for instances with staggered release times. Stronger sequential dispatching results for staggered-release instances motivate future work on learning sequential priority updates. The framework also remains interpretable, as the learned job priorities align with established heuristic principles, supported by permutation-importance analysis of input features. Overall, DGSF establishes a structured framework for integrating data-driven priority estimation with constrained optimization in single-machine scheduling, with strong potential to serve as a sequencing module within more complex multi-stage and multi-machine scheduling problems.

title: Extending the by-production approach: a shared inputs framework for modeling technologies with undesirable outputs
Dynamic capacity-constrained bin packing for capacity batching: a new framework for multi-stage steel production scheduling
Exact decomposition algorithms for the student clustering problem
Managing supply chain tensions: The strategic interaction between promoted listings and manufacturer encroachment

Pairwise comparisons meet optimal transport theory
abstract: In this paper, we reinterpret pairwise comparison theory through the lens of optimal transport. The main contribution is the connection established between pairwise comparison matrices, doubly stochastic scaling, and entropy-regularized transport problems. Using Sinkhorn scaling, we show how consistency, priority derivation, and inconsistency assessment can be studied within a common optimal-transport framework. As methodological consequences of this connection, we obtain a new characterization of consistency, a Sinkhorn-based prioritization method, and an entropy-based inconsistency index. We study these proposals both analytically and numerically, and compare them with established methods from the literature.

title: Models for the assessment of partial scale characteristics in polyhedral technologies
abstract: Partial scale characteristics of efficient frontiers include the notions of partial scale efficiency, most productive scale size and returns to scale that are evaluated with respect to some selected subsets of inputs and outputs, while keeping the remaining inputs and outputs fixed. We show that, in any polyhedral technology, all such partial characteristics can be assessed by solving linear programs based on the appropriately specified partial cone extension of the technology. We obtain a general operational statement of such cone extensions and illustrate our results by an example.

title: Competition and refurbishing strategy in closed-loop supply chains considering collection priority
The undirected circular facility layout problem
abstract: In the Undirected Circular Facility Layout Problem (UDCFLP) one has given a set of departments, their lengths and pairwise weights between the departments. The goal is to find an arrangement on a circle that minimizes the total sum of the weighted center-to-center distances, either measured in clockwise or in counter-clockwise direction, depending on which distance is shorter. Despite the advantages of circular manufacturing systems in comparison to row layout systems, the UDCFLP with arbitrary lengths has not been considered in the literature before. We present two new mixed-integer linear programming models for the UDCFLP by adapting two well-known models from well-studied facility layout problems from the literature and exploiting their connection with the UDCFLP. To strengthen our models, we study the structure of the associated polytopes. We derive different classes of cutting planes and prove their correctness. In a computational study we compare our stand-alone models and their strengthened variants regarding the deviation between their lower bounds and heuristically determined upper bounds and their computational times.

title: Traffic service provision and pricing with consumer segmentation in online retail platform
Iterated local search for coverage path planning with imperfect extended detection
abstract: Naval mines, many of which are remnants of past conflicts, still threaten ships, wildlife, and the environment. To detect these underwater mines, autonomous minesweepers can be used, e.g. a REMUS 100 autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) equipped with sidescan sonars. We frame the minesweeping task as a combinatorial optimization problem called coverage path planning with imperfect extended detection (CPPIED). An efficient solution to the CPPIED minimizes both the path length and the number of turns (in that order), while satisfying stochastic coverage constraints in a grid environment. The current state of the art is a hybrid heuristic called DpSweeper. We show that, although this algorithm rapidly produces feasible solutions, the path quality is limited by its greedy nature. Since local search algorithms are known for their capacity to improve feasible solutions to large-scale combinatorial problems, such as vehicle routing problems with spatial coverage, we propose an iterated local search heuristic to enhance the solutions generated by DpSweeper. Our heuristic reduces the path length of solutions provided by DpSweeper by 9% to 28%, and the number of turns by 19% to 42%, hence improving the planning methods for minesweeping operations and bridging vehicle routing and coverage path planning problems.

title: Adaptive threshold iterated local search: An adaptive self-parameterizing algorithm for solving sports timetabling problems of the international timetabling competition 2021
Dynamic location-routing with decentralized modular production facilities and resource collection: A Variable Neighborhood Search approach
abstract: Hydrogen is emerging as a sustainable fuel, relevant for heavy-duty vehicles such as agricultural machinery, which are prevalent in rural areas. While utilizing residual biomass, such as straw or wood, is a promising option for local bio-hydrogen production, both the residues and the hydrogen demand are typically small-scale and geographically dispersed. Coupled with limited local infrastructure, the resulting high transportation costs threaten the economic viability of bio-hydrogen. To address this challenge, we propose a flexible, decentralized bio-hydrogen supply chain network, allowing hydrogen production close to both rural customers and residues, and thereby reducing transportation costs. We formulate this concept as the Dynamic Modular Location-Routing Problem with Resource Collection and Customer Delivery (DMLRP-RCCD). Our model simultaneously optimizes production site selection, the dynamic allocation of mobile production units, resource selection, and both resource collection and customer delivery route generation over a multi-period planning horizon. To solve this highly complex problem, we develop a tailored, nested Variable Neighborhood Search metaheuristic. Extensive computational experiments across 288 instances demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of our solution approach, which achieves highly competitive and stable results compared to a state-of-the-art exact solver. Furthermore, a real-world case study confirms the practical applicability of our concept and demonstrates that dynamic, decentralized production can successfully meet local hydrogen demand. These outcomes underscore the potential of our work for the future decarbonization of heavy-duty transport in rural areas.
